summary.text: Slate is a fine-grained metamorphic rock made when shale-type sedimentary rock of clay or volcanic ash goes through low-grade regional metamorphism.
Strong compression makes its clay flakes regrow in planes at right angles to the squeeze, giving it a foliation called slaty cleavage.
Struck along those planes, many slates split into smooth flat sheets that have long been used for roofing, floor tiles and billiard tables.

facts.label: Parent rock
facts.value: Shale-type rock of clay or volcanic ash

facts.label: Main minerals
facts.value: Quartz, illite and chlorite, up to 95%

facts.label: Volume lost forming
facts.value: Up to 50% of the original mudrock

facts.label: Water absorption
facts.value: Under 0.4%, so it resists frost damage

facts.label: Roof lifespan
facts.value: Several hundred years, often with little maintenance

items.prompt: A quarry worker wants thin, flat roofing sheets from a block of slate. How should the block be struck?

options.label: Across its planes, at right angles
Parallel to its planes of foliation
Along the original mud layers
Anywhere, since slate has no planes

items.explain: Slate splits into smooth sheets when struck parallel to its foliation, and that foliation need not follow the original sedimentary layers.

items.prompt: Mud was laid down in flat layers, then later squeezed hard from one direction as it became slate. How do the slate's splitting planes tend to lie?

options.label: Parallel to the old mud layers
Parallel to the direction of the squeeze
At right angles to the squeeze
In random directions throughout

items.explain: Slaty cleavage forms in planes perpendicular to the compression, independent of the original sedimentary layering.

items.prompt: Fossils, even remains of delicate organisms, can sometimes still be found in slate. What makes that possible?

options.label: Slate forms only from fossil shells
Fossils grow inside the rock afterwards
Slate never undergoes any compression
Slate forms at fairly low heat and pressure

items.explain: Slate forms in low heat and pressure compared with most other metamorphic rocks, so some fossils survive in it.

items.prompt: Why does a slate roof hold up well through freezing winters?

options.label: It soaks up almost no water
It stays warm from the sun
It bends instead of cracking
Ice cannot form on grey stone

items.explain: Slate's water absorption index is under 0.4%, which makes it resistant to frost damage.

items.prompt: As buried mudrock is compacted and turned into slate, how much of its volume can it lose?

options.label: Almost none at all
Up to about half
Around nine tenths
It gains volume instead

items.explain: Converting mudrock to slate can involve losing up to 50% of the mudrock's volume as it is compacted.

items.prompt: Where does the everyday phrase "a clean slate" come from?

options.label: Freshly quarried roofing blocks
Roofs washed bare by rain
Billiard tables wiped before play
Small slates written on with chalk

items.explain: A writing slate was a small smooth piece of the rock used with chalk as a notepad, and the phrase comes from that use.
